newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher, 30-yr sale revives bulls.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher, 30-yr sale revives bulls.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices rallied on Thursday, erasing early losses after the Treasury's 30-year bond auction attracted unexpectedly strong demand.
The restoration of the bullish tone occurred after prices were beaten down overnight and in the first half of the trading session in New York.
What hurt the market overnight were remarks from Eisuku Sakakibara asserting that the dollar's recovery from its sharp slide last year was coming to an end, analysts said.

"The Treasury market in particular has benefitted quite a bit recently from foreign purchases and if the dollar were to take a downward turn, it would dash hopes of sustained foreign buying and might even prompt fears of selling," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co., a primary government securities dealer. "That's what happened overnight."

What seemed like bitter medicine overnight and in the early part of the New York session, however, proved to be just what the doctor ordered for the third (and last) part of the Treasury's quarterly refunding -- its 30-year bond auction.
With prices beaten lower, dealers stepped in to buy the auction, confident that they would be able to distribute the securities later and at higher prices.

Their confidence turned out to be well-founded. Treasury prices were sharply lower going into the early afternoon bidding deadline for the new 30-year bonds but they began to erase their losses after the deadline passed.
When the auction results were announced, the market erased the rest of its losses and moved higher.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond ended at 102-25/32, up 1-2/32.
The 30-year bond yield slid to 6.54 percent, its lowest closing level since March 7, from 6.62 percent on Wednesday.

The Treasury's new 30-year notes were sold at an average 6.618 percent yield and the ratio of bids received over those accepted was 2.68, "extremely high" for a 30-year auction, according to Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

The market had a small portion of fresh economic data to sift through. Early on, the Labor Department reported that new claims for unemployment insurance fell to 331,000 in the week ended November 2 from 342,000 a week earlier.
"The (jobless claims) numbers show us that the job market remains tight and this could become a concern by early next year if it leads to higher wage pressures," said Youngdahl.

"We've bounced between weekly claims numbers of 320,000 and 340,000 and this was right in the middle," said Rupkey. "This should have been a slight negative (for the Treasury market), but it didn't hurt us because we were busy dealing with (the) dollar-yen (comments)."
Margaret Patel, managing director and portfolio manager at Greenwich, Ct.-based Northstar Funds, dismissed fears of upward pressure on wages.

Just as securities markets have become internationalized, so to some extent, have labor markets, Patel contended. Competition with cheaper labor in developing countries will cap any widespread wage pressures, she said.
At the close, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.01 percent. Six-month rates ended unchanged at 5.07 percent. Year bill rates fell one basis point to 5.13 percent.
Two-year notes rose 2/32 to 100-9/32 to yield 5.72 pct. Five-year notes rose 6/32 to 101-1/32 to yield 6.01 percent.
Ten-year notes climbed 17/32 to 101-31/32, yielding 6.23 percent at the close.

Trading volume was heavy, said GovPX. By mid-afternoon, $92.7 billion in securities had traded, 37 percent more than an average autumn Thursday. Bill volume was up 34 percent and coupon trading was up 39 percent.
--North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
